claims.text: Earthquakes and volcanoes lie in long, narrow belts along plate boundaries, with the greatest cluster around the Pacific Ocean (the Pacific Ring of Fire, which holds about three quarters of the world's active volcanoes), while the interiors of plates, far from boundaries, usually have few earthquakes and no volcanoes.

claims.text: Constructive (divergent) boundaries, where plates move apart, let magma rise to build new crust, usually gentle shield volcanoes with shallow earthquakes; destructive (convergent) boundaries, where one plate subducts beneath another, feed steep strato-volcanoes and the largest earthquakes; conservative boundaries, where plates slide past one another, produce earthquakes but no volcanoes because no magma reaches the surface.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Plates move; a plate boundary is simply the line where two moving plates meet, so an answer that says the boundary itself moves, or that names the wrong setting for a named example, has confused the boundary with the plates.

claims.text: A distribution answer says where the events are, how spread out they are and where they are absent - long narrow belts, the thickest cluster around the Pacific, and gaps in the plate interiors - rather than stopping at "on plate boundaries", which describes no pattern.

claims.text: Earthquakes are caused when locked, stressed rocks at a plate boundary fracture suddenly and release their stored energy as seismic waves; volcanic eruptions happen where magma can rise to the surface, which happens readily at constructive boundaries and, more explosively, where subduction produces sticky, gas-rich magma.
